newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian grain-belt Krasnodar eyes better harvest.
newsitem.headline: Russian grain-belt Krasnodar eyes better harvest.

text.p: Grain production in Russia's fertile, farm-belt Krasnodar region, where the harvest is in full swing, is likely to stage a partial recovery on last year's disaster, local agricultural officials said on Tuesday.
But persistent rains in key growing areas could yet slow progress in the fields and hurt the quality of the key winter wheat crop.

"At this early stage, I think it is reasonable to expect a harvest here of one million tonnes more than in 1996," said Leonid Gorkovyenko, first deputy head of the production department at the Krasnodar regional adminstration.

Net grain output in this farm belt, which lies at the foothills of the Northern Caucasus mountains by the Black Sea, was only 4.52 million tonnes last year, down sharply from 5.73 million in 1995 and 9.77 million in 1990.
Gorkovyenko said the crop still faced risks, with two weeks or so still to run in this year's main harvest.
"We have already had a lot of rain this season and are seeing the quality of the wheat suffer," he said.
"Say we had yields of, say, five tonnes per sector -- after three days of rain, this could easily fall to 4.5 tonnes per hectare".
Poor output in Krasnodar, where the first harvest figures usually emerge, can put pressure on Russia's other regions to boost output.
Officials said Kranosdar suffered an unusually long winter, and severe storms in April wiped out over 100 billion roubles' worth of crops in just two days.
But overall grain quality would be far better this year compared to last year's drought-hit output.

Strenuous efforts by farmers and local administrators to secure supplies of fertilisers and machinery had shown some results and somewhat improved conditions. But shortages of inputs continued to plague the farm sector.
"This year, the situation has improved, because we put our all into it," said Vladimir Nadykta, deputy head of the administration's agriculture section.
"We'll have more high-quality grain for bread."
Krasnodar's farmers, like peasants across Russia, have found the transition from a planned, centralised economy to a scrape-by system unavoidable and painful.
"The process of decentralisation from Moscow is well underway," Nadykta said, adding that more changes were needed to ensure Russia's grain industry survived.
"The regions still need to do a lot to establish the basis for further reforms," he said, adding, "we also need to eat our own food before consuming imported goods."
Despite fertile land, with some of the best soil in places like Krasnodar and neighbouring Stavropol, Russia has struggled to feed itself in recent years and imports around 40 percent of its food.
Official forecasts peg Russia's net grain output this year at 70 million tonnes, little changed from 1996's second worst showing in three decades of 69.3 million tonnes.
But some analysts and government officials, among them First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, say recovery this year could be a more substantial 80 million tonnes.
